grades.quote: If either process tries to write into the shared page, the MMU will use an interrupt to transfer control to the operating system. The operating system can then make a copy of the page, so that the sender and receiver now have their own individual copies, which can be writable.
grades.reason: Explains the generic COW mechanism: the page is shared read-only, a write triggers an MMU interrupt to the OS, and the OS copies the page so each side gets its own writable copy. This is the isolation-preserving mechanism, but it is described for message passing rather than fork.

grades.quote: Although the child starts with a copy of the parent’s memory, the parent and child execute with separate memory and separate registers: changing a variable in one does not affect the other.
grades.reason: States the fork isolation property (parent and child have separate memory, and changes in one don't affect the other). It says nothing about copy-on-write or page sharing.

grades.quote: operating kernels optimize the implementation of fork for this use case by using virtual memory techniques such as copy-on-write (see Section 5).
grades.reason: Says fork can use copy-on-write to avoid wasteful copying before exec. It gives no detail on how sharing is kept safe (read-only mapping, copy on fault).
Covers file descriptor inheritance, I/O redirection and shared file offsets across fork. It does not cover copy-on-write or memory page sharing.
